title: Town conversations

rows.text: Town conversations
132 draft packages. Images have no embedded text; wording listed as an overlay is rendered separately.
TOWN-01-A · Pedestrian Funding Rejected
Albuquerque
At an Albuquerque bus stop, a warehouse picker studies the crew’s walking route.
Fact: In September 2025, Albuquerque said Trump’s administration tried to withdraw $11.5 million for the Rail Trail while favoring car-based projects.
Fictional resident: warehouse picker waiting for a ride — “Trump wants projects for cars.” She points at your shoes. “Put a license plate on those. We might get you a sidewalk.”
Scene: At the bus shelter, the picker holds a blank license-plate-shaped scrap above a traveler’s worn shoes; the van waits beyond the curb.
Source: Trump Administration Attempts to Cancel Money for Rail Trail (2025-09-11)
TOWN-01-B · Law and Order, Terms Apply
Albuquerque
Outside an Albuquerque laundromat, a retired machinist discusses the city’s lawsuit while the crew waits for dry clothes.
Fact: In July 2025, Albuquerque challenged Trump’s immigration conditions on police grants supporting officer salaries, evidence processing and crime-victim services.
Fictional resident: retired machine-shop worker — “Trump threatened police money over immigration. So when somebody steals my bike, should I report a theft or ask whether it crossed a border?”
Scene: The retiree gives his bicycle an extra loop of chain while a traveler sits beside laundry; focus on the ordinary lock, not a fictional arrest.
Source: City Joins Lawsuits to Block Federal Cuts to Public Safety, Housing (2025-07-11)
TOWN-01-C · A Roof With Conditions
Albuquerque
Outside an Albuquerque rental office, a grounds worker compares notices with the travelers.
Fact: Albuquerque’s July 2025 lawsuit challenged Trump administration conditions threatening housing grants that supported rental assistance, eviction prevention and rehousing.
Fictional resident: grounds worker on a break — “Immigration conditions on housing money. I rent a one-bedroom. Apparently it needs a foreign policy.”

Scene: Outside the rental office, the resident searches a normal key ring while holding a blank lease envelope; the travelers wait beside their van. An ordinary little key and plain lease envelope carry the absurd contrast with national immigration policy; no staged hazard or symbolic threat.
Source: City Joins Lawsuits to Block Federal Cuts to Public Safety, Housing (2025-07-11)
TOWN-02-A · America First, Beef Pending
Amarillo
At an Amarillo grocery picnic table, a feed-store loader notices the crew dividing a sandwich.
Fact: Texas Farm Bureau objected in October 2025 to Trump’s proposal for more Argentine beef imports, warning it could hurt Texas ranchers.
Fictional resident: feed-store loader eating lunch — “Trump’s cheaper-beef plan upset our ranchers.” He inspects his sandwich. “I’ll notify Argentina when the affordable bit arrives.”
Scene: The loader opens his sandwich and studies the thin filling with exaggerated care; a traveler checks an equally modest lunch.
Source: Suggestions to increase Argentinian beef imports harm Texas cattle ranchers (2025-10-20)
TOWN-02-B · The Government Time Clock
Amarillo
At an Amarillo diner counter, a delivery driver reads a Pantex audit beside the travelers.
Fact: A 2025 federal audit reported that Pantex contractor CNS had repaid $18.4 million in 2024 for billing the government for hours not worked.
Fictional resident: delivery driver — “Eighteen million for hours nobody worked.” He looks at your job hunt. “We’ve been asking whether they’re hiring. Ask whether they’re billing.”
Scene: The driver turns a blank audit page toward the travelers while pointing to their ordinary work gloves; no real employee is depicted or accused.
Source: Audit: DOE-OIG-25-36 (2025-11-26)
TOWN-02-C · Restart the Country
Amarillo
While the van cools in Amarillo, an appliance repairer recalls the nuclear-worker firings.
Fact: In February 2025, Trump’s administration reversed most NNSA firings; AP reported Pantex near Amarillo among the hardest-hit offices in the DOGE cuts.
Fictional resident: appliance repairer — “Fire the nuclear staff. Rehire the nuclear staff.” He points at your ignition. “Government efficiency: have we tried turning the country off and on?”
Scene: The appliance repairer points from a blank news screen to the van’s ignition while the traveler holds the keys; all remain at an ordinary public parking spot.
Source: Trump administration tries to bring back fired nuclear weapons workers in DOGE reversal (2025-02-16)
TOWN-03-A · Veterans, Please Close Your Books
Austin
Outside an Austin library, a retired delivery driver tells the travelers why a veterans’ reading group paused.
Fact: Austin-based Humanities Texas said its veterans’ reading program remained paused in May 2025 after the federal government terminated its operating grant on April 2.
Fictional resident: retired delivery driver — “The federal grant vanished. Veterans can still appear in campaign ads; apparently letting them discuss a book is where Washington draws the line.”
Scene: The resident holds an ordinary library book beside a folded veteran-event flyer; a traveler checks the library door. All print is blank.
Source: Humanities Texas: From the Director, May 2025 (2025-05)
TOWN-03-B · Public Money, Private School
Austin
At an Austin discount store, a teacher compares classroom supplies with the travelers’ grocery money.
Fact: In 2025, Texas enacted Senate Bill 2 and allocated $1 billion to education accounts that can pay for private schooling.
Fictional resident: teacher — “Texas found a billion for education accounts that cover private school. I’m buying classroom pencils. Should I put an admissions office on the pencil cup?”
Scene: Teacher holds a handful of pencils beside a small cup, jokingly setting a blank desk nameplate in front of it.
Source: Texas Education Freedom Accounts (undated)
TOWN-03-C · Feed the Pole
Austin
While you check an Austin parking meter, a bakery worker points from its timer to her ticket.
Fact: Austin’s council set the unpaid-meter fine at $75, effective March 1, 2025.
Fictional resident: a bakery worker on a delivery break — “Seventy-five dollars if the meter expires. I’m feeding it before I buy lunch. Austin has taught a pole to eat first.”

Scene: The worker holds a coin above the meter slot while her paper lunch bag hangs from her other hand; a traveler checks the meter. The upright meter receives its coin at mouth height while the lunch bag waits below.
Editable overlays: “Unpaid meter: $75” — Beside the blank ticket, as an editable callout.
Source: Austin council document setting the unpaid-meter fine (2025-02-13)
TOWN-04-A · Federal Pastry Inspection
Billings
At a Billings supermarket, a shelf stocker compares a protein bar with a pastry beside the travelers.
Fact: In May 2026, Montana announced federal approval for SNAP restrictions covering candy and prepared desserts while protecting protein bars and fresh baked goods.

Fictional resident: grocery stocker shopping after a shift — “USDA approved Montana’s food ban, with exceptions for protein bars and fresh baked goods. Hunger is simple. Your snack now needs a classification hearing.”
Scene: The stocker places the two unmarked foods on opposite sides of a shopping basket as if presiding over a tiny hearing.
Source: USDA Approves Montana SNAP Food-Restriction Waiver (2026-05-19)
TOWN-04-B · Relief Lives Upstairs
Billings
Outside a Billings apartment building, a cleaner checks a state tax notice while the travelers ask directions.
Fact: Montana’s 2026 property-tax changes give qualifying primary residences and long-term rental properties a reduced rate, including eligible properties in Billings.
Fictional resident: cleaner — “Montana’s tax break includes long-term rental properties. My landlord gets the relief. I’m hoping he lets me look at it during the next inspection.”
Scene: A cleaner folds a plain state notice beside apartment mailboxes while the travelers hold their road map.
Source: 2026 Tax Information for Montana Property Owners (undated)
TOWN-04-C · Small Government, Fabric Division
Billings
Near a Billings public building, a seamstress waits beside the travelers with some mending.
Fact: Montana’s 2025 House Bill 819 restricted which flags could be displayed on government property, including public schools and state buildings.
Fictional resident: seamstress — “Montana’s lawmakers restricted the flags government can fly. My sewing machine has more settings than the state’s idea of freedom.”
Scene: The seamstress holds a fan of colorful fabric swatches against a plain government flagpole; no flag lettering or insignia is embedded.
Source: Montana House Bill 819, 2025 (2025)
TOWN-05-A · Your Freeze Was Canceled
Boise
At a Boise laundromat, a university mailroom worker reads an old funding update beside the travelers.
Fact: On January 30, 2025, Boise State said the Trump administration’s funding-freeze memo was withdrawn, while other executive orders still required reviews of affected awards.
Fictional resident: university mailroom worker — “Trump’s funding freeze was withdrawn, but the other orders still needed checking. Washington canceled the padlock and left the chain.”
Scene: The worker closes a blank news page while a traveler untangles a laundry bag’s drawstring; a closed machine door echoes the funding uncertainty.
Source: Boise State: Federal Funding Update, January 30, 2025 (2025-01-30)
TOWN-05-B · The Rainbow Has Paperwork
Boise
Outside Boise City Hall, a delivery rider tells the travelers about the 2025 flag dispute.
Fact: In May 2025, Boise made the Pride flag an official city flag after Idaho restricted government flag displays.
Fictional resident: delivery rider — “Idaho restricted flags, so Boise made Pride official. The rainbow had to get a government job before the state would let it be seen.”
Scene: The rider points from City Hall to a small rainbow cloth tucked beside a blank document folder; scene depicts discussion, not a current flag-status claim.
Source: Salt Lake City and Boise make pride flags official city emblems, skirting flag ban laws (2025-05-07)
TOWN-05-C · The Governor’s School Supplies
Boise
At a Boise grocery store, a classroom aide compares fundraiser cookies with the travelers’ cheap lunch.
Fact: In February 2025, Idaho Governor Brad Little signed House Bill 93, creating a $50 million Parental Choice Tax Credit program.
Fictional resident: classroom aide — “Governor Little found fifty million for school-choice tax credits. Our fundraiser has oatmeal raisin. Clearly we hired the wrong lobbyist.”
Scene: The aide holds a plain tray of fundraiser cookies at a public storefront table; travelers pause with some food. Do not imply an actual school’s finances.
Source: Gov. Little signs House Bill 93 creating the Parental Choice Tax Credit program (2025-02-27)
TOWN-06-A · The Market Has Favorites
Cheyenne
At a Cheyenne hardware store, a roofer discusses a state press release with the travelers.
Fact: In July 2025, Wyoming Secretary of State Chuck Gray praised Trump’s order ending wind and solar subsidies while championing coal, oil and gas.
Fictional resident: roofer — “Gray cheered Trump for ending wind and solar subsidies, then cheered coal and oil. A free market, with the secretary of state holding the scorecards.”
Scene: Roofer compares a plain solar-roof brochure and a fuel receipt; the travelers hold a small shopping basket.
Source: Wyoming Secretary of State Praises Order to End Wind and Solar Subsidies (2025-07-09)
TOWN-06-B · Please Introduce Yourself to Your Government
Cheyenne
At a Cheyenne copy shop, a shift worker waits beside the travelers with some registration paperwork.
Fact: In March 2025, Wyoming enacted House Bill 156 requiring proof of U.S. citizenship and residency for voter registration; Secretary of State Chuck Gray celebrated it.
Fictional resident: shift worker — “Gray wanted more proof of citizenship and residency. The government I’ve paid for all these years would like an introduction. Should I bring flowers?”
Scene: Worker squares a plain folder on the copy counter beside a traveler’s single road map; a small vase provides the understated flowers punchline.
Source: Secretary Gray Celebrates Proof-of-Citizenship and Residency Voting Law (2025-03-21)
TOWN-06-C · The State Has a Roofing Budget
Cheyenne
Near Wyoming’s Capitol, a roofer shares a lunch bench with the travelers.
Fact: Wyoming’s government repaired its Capitol dome and applied gold leaf imported from Italy during the restoration described in 2019.
Fictional resident: roofer — “The state covered its dome in Italian gold. I patch my roof with tar. The difference, apparently, is which one of us writes the budget.”
Scene: The roofer rolls a small patch of plain roofing material between work-worn hands, with the Capitol dome visible behind.
Source: A History of the Wyoming Capitol (2019-06-04)
TOWN-07-A · Next Stop, Federal Court
Chicago
At a Chicago station entrance, a hotel cleaner compares train routes with the travelers.
Fact: CTA sued Trump’s federal transportation agencies in March 2026 over money paused for its Red Line Extension and Red and Purple Modernization projects.
Fictional resident: hotel cleaner — “Trump’s agencies paused the train money. CTA sued. Apparently the Red Line needs a transfer through federal court before it can reach another neighborhood.”
Scene: Cleaner traces a route on a blank transit map beside the station entrance; the travelers stand with their small bags.
Source: CTA Sues Over Paused Red Line Extension and Modernization Funding (2026-03-20)
TOWN-07-B · An Unrequested Ride
Chicago
At a Chicago corner store, a delivery driver discusses Trump’s attempted Guard deployment with the travelers.
Fact: In December 2025, the Supreme Court kept Trump’s attempted National Guard deployment to the Chicago area blocked while litigation continued.
Fictional resident: delivery driver — “Trump tried to send troops; the courts said wait. I can’t park here without permission, but the president thought the whole city was his loading zone.”
Scene: Driver carries an ordinary delivery bag past the travelers’ van, parked at a legal curb; no actual military presence is depicted.
Source: Supreme Court keeps Trump’s National Guard deployment blocked in the Chicago area, for now (2025-12-23)
TOWN-07-C · The Fare That Stayed Put
Chicago
At a Chicago bus stop, a grocery clerk counts change beside the travelers.
Fact: After Illinois passed a transit-funding bill, CTA approved its 2026 budget without fare increases, service cuts or layoffs.
Fictional resident: grocery clerk — “Illinois passed transit funding, so CTA avoided the fare hike. Incredible technology: legislators release money and ordinary people get to keep some.”
Scene: The clerk puts an extra coin back into a pocket beside a waiting bus; signs and fare display are blank.
Source: Chicago Transit Board Approves 2026 CTA Budget (2025-11-12)
TOWN-08-A · The Ladder Budget
Cleveland
Outside a Cleveland school, a lunchroom worker talks with the travelers during dismissal.
Fact: Representative Shontel Brown said Trump’s administration notified Cleveland schools that GEAR UP college-access funding would end September 30, 2025.

Fictional resident: school lunchroom worker — “Trump’s administration cut GEAR UP, the program helping students toward college. The ladder is still available; Washington just repossessed the bottom rungs.”
Scene: Lunchroom worker holds a student-resource leaflet beside an ordinary short stepladder used to reach the noticeboard; no child is placed at risk.
Source: Brown Calls for Restoration of Terminated Ohio Education Grants (2025)
TOWN-08-B · The Patriotic River
Cleveland
On a Cleveland riverwalk, a dock worker recalls the Cuyahoga fires as the travelers stop for water.
Fact: The Cuyahoga burned in Cleveland in 1969. Trump’s March 2025 history directive called for changes to federal historical presentations under his administration’s account of American greatness.
Fictional resident: dock worker — “Trump wants federal history restored to greatness. Our river caught fire. Should the caption say American water was working twice as hard?”
Scene: The worker holds a plain water bottle against the river view while a traveler glances at a blank historical panel; no present fire is depicted.
Source: National Park Service: The 1969 Cuyahoga River Fire (2022-05-03)
Source: White House history intervention (2025-03)
TOWN-08-C · Taxpayers Keep the River Wet
Cleveland
At a Cleveland riverside bench, a retired sewer worker shares lunch space with the travelers.
Fact: Before the famous 1969 river fire, Cleveland voters approved a $100 million bond issue in 1968 for sewer construction and water-treatment upgrades.

Fictional resident: retired sewer worker — “Cleveland voters approved the cleanup money before the famous river fire. A hundred million to keep water wet. Industry’s contribution had been making it flammable.”
Scene: Retired sewer worker rests a battered lunch tin beside a clear view of the river; ordinary residents occupy a space improved through public spending.
Source: National Park Service: The 1969 Cuyahoga River Fire (2022-05-03)
TOWN-09-A · Your Fever Is Optional
Columbia
At a Columbia laundromat, a restaurant dishwasher waits beside the travelers.
Fact: Governor Mike Kehoe signed legislation ending Missouri’s paid-sick-leave requirement in August 2025; Columbia employers could still choose to provide it.
Fictional resident: restaurant dishwasher — “Governor Kehoe ended Missouri’s paid-sick-leave requirement. My fever can still stay home. It just needs to find somebody else to pay the rent.”
Scene: Dishwasher folds a plain work apron beside a laundry basket; travelers compare their remaining grocery money. No actual sick food handling is shown.
Source: Governor Kehoe Signs Tax Cuts and Business Legislation (2025-07-10)
Source: When do employees stop earning paid sick time due to HB567? (undated)
TOWN-09-B · Prices May Continue
Columbia
At a Columbia grocery checkout, a retail stocker talks with the travelers while waiting in line.
Fact: Missouri’s 2025 law retained the scheduled $15 minimum wage but removed automatic inflation adjustments, affecting covered workers in Columbia and across the state.
Fictional resident: retail stocker — “Kehoe kept the fifteen-dollar minimum but removed its inflation adjustment. Somebody tell the groceries. They don’t appear to have received the freeze notice.”
Scene: Stocker and travelers look at a modest basket and a blank shelf ticket; no invented measured price increase is asserted.
Source: Governor Kehoe Signs Tax Cuts and Business Legislation (2025-07-10)
TOWN-09-C · Income Without the Shift
Columbia
At a Columbia bus shelter, a janitor opens a pay envelope beside the travelers.
Fact: Governor Kehoe signed a 2025 Missouri law allowing individuals to deduct federally reported capital gains from state taxable income; it applies to eligible Columbia taxpayers.
Fictional resident: janitor — “Kehoe gave individual capital gains a state income-tax deduction. I clean floors for money. Apparently I should sell the building while someone else cleans it.”
Scene: Janitor holds a plain pay envelope with a mop handle beside the bench; the travelers look toward an office building across the street.
Source: Governor Kehoe Signs Tax Cuts and Business Legislation (2025-07-10)
TOWN-10-A · The Bench Is Retiring Too
Cumberland
Beside Cumberland’s canal, a maintenance worker talks with the travelers over lunch.
Fact: After national park firings under Trump in 2025, the C&O Canal separately reported five early retirements, including its only carpenter and arborist.
Fictional resident: maintenance worker — “Trump cut park staff nationally. Here the only carpenter took early retirement. If that bench collapses, we’ll call it a successful transition to meadow.”
Scene: The resident tests a normal bench with a cautious hand before sitting; no documented structural defect is claimed.
Source: WTOP: What Budget Cuts and Reduced Staffing Could Mean for the NPS (2025-07-01)
Source: DOGE and national park staffing (2025-02)
TOWN-10-B · Destination by Executive Order
Cumberland
At Cumberland’s canal terminus, a delivery driver compares the travelers’ map with the waterway.
Fact: The C&O Canal ended at Cumberland without reaching Ohio. Trump’s January 2025 order renamed the Gulf of Mexico for federal use, without moving its shores.
Fictional resident: delivery driver — “This canal never reached Ohio. Trump renamed the Gulf. Call your van Washington and you’re there. Still out of gas, but geographically victorious.”
Scene: Driver taps the van roof while the travelers hold a map beside the canal’s actual western terminus.
Source: NPS: Canal Construction (2021-09-18)
Source: Gulf renaming (2025-01)
TOWN-10-C · Please Postpone Your Family
Cumberland
At a Cumberland supermarket, a home-care aide discusses Maryland’s leave timetable with the travelers.
Fact: Maryland’s October 2025 guidance put its new family-and-medical-leave benefits, including for eligible Cumberland workers, on a timetable beginning by January 3, 2028.
Fictional resident: home-care aide — “Maryland’s new paid family leave starts in 2028. I’ll tell my mother to schedule her recovery around the government’s recovery from scheduling.”
Scene: Home-care aide balances groceries and a plain appointment calendar at the checkout; no identifiable patient information is visible.
Source: Maryland FAMLI Frequently Asked Questions (2025-10)
TOWN-11-A · Room-Temperature Innovation
Dallas
Outside a Dallas medical campus, a lab cleaner shares a shaded lunch table.
Fact: In February 2025, Dallas’s UT Southwestern warned that the Trump administration’s proposed NIH overhead cap could cost it more than $100 million a year.

Fictional resident: a medical-campus cleaner on a lunch break — “They call freezers overhead. Let a senator keep his lunch at room temperature and see how fast overhead becomes critical infrastructure.”
Scene: A cleaner keeps a modest lunch in an insulated bag while the travelers eat nearby; sun falls across the unshaded half of the table.
Source: Proposed NIH overhead cap (2025-02-09)
TOWN-11-B · Bring Your Own House
Dallas
At a Dallas laundromat, a renter compares housing costs while the van blankets dry.
Fact: Texas law exempts $140,000 of a qualifying residence homestead’s value from school taxes. The applicant must own an interest in the home and live there.
Fictional resident: a warehouse worker who rents an apartment — “Texas has tax relief for your home. First, own one. I checked: my security deposit does not count as a down payment on freedom.”
Scene: A renter folds towels beside a small envelope of housing paperwork; a traveler checks the nearly empty laundry coin cup.
Source: Texas Comptroller: Property Tax Exemptions (undated)
TOWN-11-C · Ask the Bouncer
Dallas
A Dallas warehouse worker is reading the federal Google ruling at a library computer. He lets your crew go first; finding how to change his default search engine has used the rest of his break.

Fact: A September 2, 2025 federal ruling barred specified exclusive Google distribution contracts and ordered certain data and search-service remedies. It did not order Chrome sold or ban all distribution payments; appeals remain a separate question.

Fictional resident: a warehouse worker using a public library computer — “A court had to tell Google to leave room for other search engines. I searched Google for the exit. Felt like asking the bouncer for directions to another pub.”

Scene: At a Dallas public library, a warehouse worker has stepped aside from a blank-screen computer for currently present travelers. His lunch bag remains closed and a wall clock has a blank face. No real interface or search-result text is embedded.
Source: Justice Department Wins Significant Remedies Against Google (2025-09-02)
TOWN-12-A · Reimbursement Pending
Denver
At a Denver bus shelter, a kitchen worker tells you about the city’s unpaid federal bill.
Fact: In April 2025, FEMA denied Denver about $24 million in reimbursement for migrant services the city had already provided.

Fictional resident: a restaurant kitchen worker — “Washington said help the arrivals, then refused the reimbursement. I tried that with my landlord: patriotic housing partnership. He still wants the rent.”
Scene: A worker holds a folded expense envelope while travelers balance some food on their knees at a bus shelter; an empty envelope lies beside the full lunch bag.
Source: Denverite: What Losing $24M of Federal Money Really Means for Denver (2025-04-29)
TOWN-12-B · Please Vote Again
Denver
Over food outside a Denver grocery, a warehouse worker explains Colorado’s extra union ballot.
Fact: In May 2025, Governor Jared Polis vetoed a bill removing Colorado’s second-election requirement for negotiating a union-security agreement.
Fictional resident: a warehouse worker — “Polis kept the second vote for a union security agreement. Funny: when the boss announces a pay freeze, we never get a first vote.”
Scene: A warehouse worker eats beside a traveler; two blank ballot envelopes sit next to a single thin pay envelope, with no lettering in the artwork.
Source: Colorado General Assembly: SB25-005 Worker Protection Collective Bargaining (2025-05-16)
TOWN-12-C · Exact Change of Policy
Denver
Near the Denver Mint, a grocery clerk compares the coins in your palms.
Fact: Trump ordered an end to circulating penny production in 2025. Denver had made the coins; existing pennies remain legal tender.
Fictional resident: an off-duty grocery clerk — “Trump stopped making pennies. The price tags still end in ninety-nine. Apparently the smallest government service was giving me my change.”
Scene: A grocery clerk and a traveler search separate palms for a tiny coin near the Mint; all coins are plain discs with no numerals or lettering.
Source: AP: US Mint presses final pennies as production ends (2025-11-12)
Source: US Mint: Penny (2025)
TOWN-13-A · Apples Await Orders
Des Moines
At a Des Moines produce stall, a delivery worker points to the unsold apples.
Fact: In 2025, Trump’s USDA ended two Iowa local-food purchasing programs. One orchard needed new buyers for 50,000 pounds of apples.

Fictional resident: a produce delivery worker — “Trump’s USDA canceled the local-food programs. The apples still passed inspection. Unfortunately, they failed the new test: being lunch for someone who needs it.”
Scene: A delivery worker leans on a handcart beside full apple crates while travelers buy some food; no crates carry labels.
Source: Radio Iowa: Farmers Feel the Impact of Local Food Programs Being Eliminated (2025-04-02)
TOWN-13-B · The Light Switch Veto
Des Moines
At a Des Moines laundromat, a bus driver holds an electric bill up to the window beside your folding table.
Fact: Des Moines’s electric franchise fee rose to 7.5% in 2025.

Fictional resident: a bus driver doing laundry on a day off — “City gets seven and a half percent when I turn on a lamp. I read the bill by the window now. The sun hasn’t signed a franchise agreement.”

Scene: The driver tilts an unlettered utility bill into the sunbeam while a traveler sorts the crew’s own laundry nearby. A switched-off lamp stands beside the bill; sunlight does the job from outside the building.
Editable overlays: “City franchise fee: 7.5%” — Beside the blank utility bill.
Source: Des Moines electric-franchise ordinance 16,485 (2025)
TOWN-13-C · Need-Based, Need Optional
Des Moines
At a Des Moines grocery exit, a school cook pauses beside your modest food purchase.
Fact: Starting in the 2025–26 school year, Iowa removed income limits for its state-funded education savings accounts for accredited private-school expenses.
Fictional resident: a public-school cook — “Iowa’s private-school accounts no longer have an income ceiling. Finally, a billionaire can get tuition help without the indignity of needing it.”
Scene: A school cook carries a small bag of food past a sleek luxury car in a grocery lot; the travelers count change at their van.
Source: Iowa Department of Education: Students First Education Savings Accounts (undated)
TOWN-14-A · The Card Can Sit Down
El Paso
At an El Paso streetcar stop, a grocery clerk watches a visitor hunt through a wallet beside you.
Fact: El Paso’s Sun Metro streetcar is fare-free.
Fictional resident: a grocery clerk waiting for the streetcar — “City streetcar’s free. You can tell who’s new: they board with their card out, like they’re feeding a nervous horse.”

Scene: A visitor extends an unmarked card gingerly toward the open doorway while the grocery clerk gestures them aboard; a current traveler waits nearby. The visitor approaches the harmless open door with the cautious arm position used to feed a horse.
Editable overlays: “Streetcar: FREE” — On the blank platform information panel.
Source: Sun Metro: About the Streetcars (undated)
TOWN-14-B · Dress the Fridge for Subsidies
El Paso
While you ask about a charging cable, an El Paso repair-shop owner holds a necktie against a refrigerator.
Fact: El Paso’s December 2023 Meta agreement offered an 80% city property-tax rebate for its first phase, conditioned on $800 million investment and 50 jobs.
Fictional resident: an appliance repair-shop owner — “Meta can get eighty percent of its city property tax back. I’m putting a tie on the fridge. One of us is going to qualify.”

Scene: The owner holds a necktie against the refrigerator’s handle while a traveler points to a charging cable on the counter. The refrigerator is being dressed as the applicant most likely to obtain an economic-development deal.
Editable overlays: “Meta deal: 80% city property-tax rebate” — Detached callout above the refrigerator.; “Conditions apply” — Beneath the rebate callout.
Source: City of El Paso: Data Centers (undated)
TOWN-14-C · Return to Sender
El Paso
At an El Paso grocery exit, a stocker watches you total the cost of some supplies.
Fact: El Paso sits on the Mexican border. New York Fed researchers found US firms and consumers bore most of the cost of Trump’s 2025 tariffs.
Fictional resident: an off-duty grocery stocker — “Trump says foreigners pay his tariffs. I tried handing my grocery bill across the bridge. They handed it back. Excellent border security.”
Scene: An off-duty stocker holds a small grocery receipt near the pedestrian approach to a distant international bridge; the travelers compare their shopping bag with their remaining cash.
Source: Trump tariffs passed to Americans (2026-02)
Source: National Park Service: Chamizal History and Culture (undated)
TOWN-15-A · Stop Watching the Water
Flagstaff
At a Flagstaff picnic table, a plumber hears you discussing water for the next stretch.
Fact: Trump’s 2025 budget proposal would close Flagstaff’s Grand Canyon Monitoring and Research Center, threatening research used to manage the Colorado River and Glen Canyon Dam.
Fictional resident: a residential plumber — “Trump proposed closing the canyon’s river-monitoring center. If I stopped checking leaks to save money, I would be called a former plumber.”
Scene: A plumber refills a small water jug beside travelers at a picnic table; a loose faucet drips visibly into a basin.
Source: KJZZ: Proposal Threatens Grand Canyon Monitoring and Research Center (2025-06-18)
TOWN-15-B · Pluto, Pending Appropriation
Flagstaff
Outside a Flagstaff stargazing event, a mechanic steadies a battered amateur telescope.
Fact: Flagstaff’s Lowell Observatory discovered Pluto. Trump’s April 2026 budget proposal sought a 47% cut to NASA science; Congress would determine the actual funding.

Fictional resident: an auto mechanic who enjoys stargazing — “Trump proposed cutting NASA science almost in half. We found Pluto with a telescope. His budget committee could lose it with a calculator.”
Scene: A mechanic steadies a small telescope with a folded scrap of cardboard while one traveler looks upward; the open sky dwarfs the improvised equipment.
Source: American Astronomical Society: Policy Update, 8 April 2026 (2026-04-08)
Source: Lowell Observatory: This Week in Astronomy History, February 15–21 (undated)
TOWN-15-C · Government Overreach, Upward
Flagstaff
On a Flagstaff evening walk, a night cleaner stops where the stars show above the shops.
Fact: Flagstaff adopted an outdoor-lighting ordinance in 1958, using city regulation to protect the night sky for residents and observatories.
Fictional resident: a night cleaner — “Flagstaff regulated outdoor lighting so we could see the stars. Terrible government interference. A billboard might have sold that sky something.”
Scene: Shielded streetlights pool light on the sidewalk while an unlettered billboard remains dim below a clear star field; a cleaner and traveler look above it.
Source: City of Flagstaff: Dark Sky (undated)
TOWN-16-A · Mop Up the Savings
Frederick
At a Frederick sandwich counter, a hospital porter discusses Trump’s announced federal health cuts.

TOWN-33-B · Freedom Has a Boundary
Salt Lake City

TOWN-33-C · The Rainbow Filed Its Paperwork
Salt Lake City
Near Salt Lake City Hall, a seamstress pauses while you rest on the steps.
Fact: In May 2025, Salt Lake City adopted new official Pride, transgender and Juneteenth-themed city flags after Utah restricted which flags government buildings could display.
Fictional resident: a seamstress — “Utah tried banning unofficial flags. The city made Pride flags official. The rainbow is still here; it just had to pass a municipal background check.”

Source: AP: Salt Lake City and Boise Adopt Official Pride Flags (2025-05-07)
TOWN-34-A · The Children Continue Anyway
San Antonio
At a San Antonio playground bench, a school aide discusses the federal funding freeze.
Fact: During Trump’s January 2025 federal funding-freeze confusion, San Antonio ISD said affected programs would continue while it awaited state and federal guidance.

Fictional resident: a school aide on a break — “Trump froze funding; the district kept programs running while waiting for instructions. The children also kept being children. Terrible failure to coordinate with Washington.”

TOWN-34-B · The Tuition Has a State Escort
San Antonio
At a San Antonio grocery queue, a bus driver adds pencils to a small food purchase.
Fact: Governor Abbott signed Texas’s education savings-account program in 2025, with $1 billion in initial state funding for eligible private-education expenses.

Fictional resident: a school bus driver and parent — “Abbott gave private-school accounts a billion-dollar launch. My child’s classroom still requests pencils. I should have sent the supply list to a lobbyist.”
Scene: A school bus driver places loose pencils beside a small grocery bag while travelers count cash; no invented school budget chart is depicted.
Source: Texas Education Freedom Accounts (2026)
TOWN-34-C · The Fee Passed Inspection
San Antonio
At a San Antonio garage, a mechanic taps a registration receipt while you ask about the new rules.
Fact: Texas ended most noncommercial vehicle safety inspections in January 2025 but kept a $7.50 replacement fee; emissions and commercial inspection requirements remain.
Fictional resident: an independent mechanic — “They scrapped most safety inspections and kept the fee. The car stays outside. Open your wallet and say ‘ah.’”

TOWN-35-A · The Groceries Need a Hearing
Sioux Falls

Fact: In July 2025, Feeding South Dakota asked state lawmakers for $3 million after Trump-era federal cuts reduced its food supply across the state.

Fictional resident: a food delivery worker — “Federal cuts left Feeding South Dakota asking legislators for three million. Hunger now needs a committee hearing. It has prepared some very brief stomach remarks.”
Scene: A delivery worker rests an empty food cart beside travelers eating a modest lunch; a closed plain folder sits where a full food tray might fit.
Source: Feeding South Dakota asks South Dakota lawmakers for $3M due to federal cuts (2025-07-30)
TOWN-35-B · The State Came for Dinner
Sioux Falls
At a Sioux Falls grocery checkout, a school cook separates onions from a sprawling receipt.
Fact: South Dakota voters rejected Initiated Measure 28 in 2024. It proposed barring state taxes on many human-consumption goods, excluding alcohol and prepared food.
Fictional resident: a school cook shopping for dinner — “The grocery-tax repeal lost. State still comes to dinner. Never chops an onion, never washes a plate, always gets served before I do.”

Source: South Dakota 2024 General Election Ballot Question Pamphlet (2024)
TOWN-35-C · Try Asking the Landowner
Sioux Falls
At a Sioux Falls feed-store bench, a farmhand discusses the state’s pipeline law.
Fact: In March 2025, Governor Rhoden barred eminent domain for carbon-oxide pipelines in South Dakota, preventing compulsory land acquisition for those projects while allowing voluntary deals.

Scene: A farmhand rests a pair of muddy boots beside a feed-store bench while travelers examine a simple unlettered field map; no real property boundary is reproduced.

South Bend
At a South Bend café, a campus kitchen worker tells you about Notre Dame’s budget notice.

Fictional resident: a university kitchen worker — “Trump’s funding and tax uncertainty put campus hiring on ice. The dishes still arrive hot. Washington has created a hiring freeze with excellent steam.”

TOWN-36-B · Retirement Must Outlive Management
South Bend
Outside South Bend’s auto museum, a retired machinist shares a bench with you.
Fact: Studebaker’s 1963 closure left nearly 3,000 South Bend workers without pension benefits, fueling reform. Congress’s 1974 ERISA law later set minimum standards for private retirement plans.

Fictional resident: a retired machinist — “Congress tightened pension rules after Studebaker workers lost benefits. Revolutionary idea: retirement money should survive the company’s final management decision.”
Scene: A retired machinist holds a closed pension folder beside a modest lunch bag; an old factory photograph is displayed without captions near the museum entrance.

Source: US Department of Labor: ERISA (undated)
TOWN-36-C · The Endowment Seeks Absolution
South Bend
At a South Bend grocery bench, a campus cleaner compares bank fees with the university’s tax fight.
Fact: In 2025, Notre Dame joined other faith-based institutions seeking a religious exemption from higher endowment-return taxes. The final federal legislation included no such exemption.
Fictional resident: a university cleaner — “Notre Dame sought religious relief on investment taxes. I asked if my overdraft was also a matter of faith. The bank believes in fees.”
Scene: A campus cleaner studies a small bank envelope beside a grocery bag; the university’s distant grand buildings contrast with the ordinary bench.
Source: Notre Dame’s Response to Federal Funding Cuts (2025-10-28)
TOWN-37-A · The Heat Survived the Cut
Spokane

Fact: In September 2025, Spokane reported that Trump’s administration rescinded a $19.9 million grant supporting planned heating, cooling and air-filter improvements for 300 low-income homes.

Fictional resident: a grocery worker who rents an apartment — “Trump’s administration rescinded the home-cooling grant. The heat kept its funding. I am applying to become a federally recognized breeze.”
Scene: A renter fans themself with a blank paper at a shaded bus stop while travelers share some water; windows of nearby modest homes remain closed against outdoor haze.

TOWN-37-B · The Ceiling Still Goes Up
Spokane
At a Spokane laundromat, a delivery worker compares a rent notice with a pay slip.
Fact: Governor Bob Ferguson signed Washington’s rent-stabilization law in May 2025, limiting increases for covered existing tenants to 7% plus inflation or 10%, whichever is lower.
Fictional resident: a delivery worker — “Ferguson capped rent hikes. Good. My landlord’s ceiling now rises more slowly than before, which is helpful because my paycheck still cannot reach it.”
Scene: A delivery worker holds a blank lease notice below a high laundromat ceiling while a small pay envelope rests on the folding table beside travelers’ laundry.

Source: Washington Commerce: HB1217 Resource Center (undated)

Spokane

Fictional resident: a warehouse worker — “Job agencies sold lousy jobs; workers complained. Spokane restricted street speaking. The city solved the employment problem by regulating the people describing it.”
Scene: A warehouse worker and traveler sit beside an empty street corner where a small wooden speaking box remains as an unlettered historical prop.

Springfield, IL

Fictional resident: a building cleaner — “Congress shut down government and Lincoln tours closed. You could admire democracy through the window. Please do not touch; it was a display model.”

Springfield, IL
At a Springfield grocery checkout, an off-duty stocker compares your food total with an hourly wage.

Source: Illinois Department of Labor: Minimum Wage FAQ (2025)
TOWN-39-A · Protein Was Not Renewed
Springfield, MO

Springfield, MO

St. Louis

Fictional resident: a trophy engraver — “He wants world peace on a bowling trophy. I charge by the letter. We’re negotiating a ceasefire.”

St. Louis

Fact: St. Louis lists a $20 meter fine that doubles after 30 days and reaches $80 after 45 days.

Fictional resident: a delivery driver sorting personal paperwork — “Twenty dollars grows into eighty in forty-five days. I keep the ticket next to my savings statement. Maybe it’ll teach it something.”

TOWN-41-A · Boots on Layaway
Toledo

At a Toledo bus stop, a warehouse supervisor tells your crew how the 2024 court ruling killed the higher federal overtime salary threshold. He’d already picked out replacement work boots. They’re still in the shop, enjoying his time off.

Fictional resident: a salaried warehouse supervisor — “Those boots were going to see forty hours a week. Now they get Sundays, evenings and every federal holiday. Best job in the warehouse.”

Scene: A salaried warehouse supervisor at a Toledo public bus stop shows currently present travelers a blank footwear catalog. His worn work boots are in the foreground; new boots may appear only as a small clearly illustrative catalog image, not an acquired item.

TOWN-41-B · Lost Money Found a Stadium
Toledo
At a Toledo diner, a cleaner recalls Ohio’s decision to use unclaimed funds for football.
Fact: Governor Mike DeWine’s 2025 Ohio budget set aside $600 million in unclaimed funds for a new Cleveland Browns stadium, making a statewide fund part of the stadium plan.

Fictional resident: a building cleaner — “DeWine put unclaimed money toward the Browns’ stadium. I lose twenty dollars and retrace my steps. Ohio finds six hundred million and buys football architecture.”
Scene: A cleaner searches an old coat pocket beside a diner booth while travelers eat; the television shows only a blank football-field graphic with no teams or scores.
Source: AP: Ohio Budget Includes Stadium Funding (2025-07-01)
TOWN-41-C · The Public Bought Back the Ground
Toledo
At Toledo’s Glass City Metropark, a groundskeeper rests while you share some food.
Fact: In 2022 and 2023, Metroparks Toledo used clean harbor-dredged sediment to help restore former industrial ground at Glass City Metropark and its Riverwalk.

Fictional resident: a park groundskeeper — “Metroparks used clean harbor mud to rebuild industrial ground. Government turned dredging into a park. Industry had spent years demonstrating the reverse procedure.”
Scene: A groundskeeper sits beside travelers where young grasses meet an older industrial wall; a plain sediment sample jar is closed on the worker’s cart.
Source: Removal Recommendation: Restrictions on Navigational Dredging Activities in the Maumee Area of Concern (2024-08-20)
TOWN-42-A · Refresh to Remain Employed
Tucson
At a Tucson shaded food stop, a city maintenance worker checks a blank phone screen.
Fact: Tucson’s April 2025 budget memo reported federal grant portals repeatedly shutting and reopening under Trump; nearly 200 grant-funded jobs could be at risk if support disappeared.

Fictional resident: a city maintenance worker on a break — “Trump’s grant portals kept shutting. Nearly two hundred jobs faced funding risk. New job description: convince a website that Tucson still exists.”
Scene: A maintenance worker refreshes a phone with a blank screen under an awning while travelers share some water; the shade is narrow but usable.
Source: City of Tucson: Recommended Fiscal Year 2026 Budget, April 22 Study Session (2025-04-22)
TOWN-42-B · The Country Club Gets the Second Sip
Tucson
At a Tucson park drinking fountain, a groundskeeper explains the separate irrigation system.
Fact: Tucson invested in reclaimed water in 1984 to reduce groundwater use. Its municipal system sends treated wastewater to irrigate parks, schools, golf courses and cemeteries.
Fictional resident: a park groundskeeper — “The city sends treated wastewater to parks and golf courses. Sensible. The country club can have my old water; I am keeping the first sip.”
Scene: A groundskeeper stands by a visibly separate closed irrigation valve while a traveler fills drinking water at the fountain; no cross-connection or unsafe use is depicted.
Source: Reclaimed Water — City of Tucson (undated)
TOWN-42-C · The Pentagon Needs a Parts Tray
Tucson
At a Tucson public overlook near the aircraft-storage area, a mechanic shares a snack with you.

Fact: Tucson’s military aircraft yard salvages reusable parts. In March 2025, senior Trump officials, including Pete Hegseth, discussed military strike plans in a Signal chat that accidentally included a journalist.
Fictional resident: an auto mechanic — “I count spare bolts before a repair. Hegseth’s strike-planning chat included a journalist. Maybe the Pentagon needs one of my little trays.”
Scene: A mechanic closes a small divided tray of plain spare bolts at a public overlook; stored aircraft remain behind a distant secure fence while travelers eat nearby.
Source: Signal airstrike chat (2025-03)
Source: Davis-Monthan Air Force Base: America’s Airpower Reservoir (2021)
TOWN-43-A · Preventive Medicine, Presidential Forecast
Tulsa
At a Tulsa clinic’s outdoor bench, a cleaner discusses the health department’s funding worries.
Fact: In March 2025, Tulsa health officials faced uncertainty over Trump-era federal support. Grants had provided over $13 million, about 30% of department revenue, in fiscal 2023–24.
Fictional resident: a clinic cleaner — “Trump’s cuts have health officials guessing what Washington will fund. I asked whether uncertainty is contagious. They need a grant to find out.”
Scene: A cleaner waits on a clinic’s outdoor bench with a small lunch bag; travelers leave space beside a plain appointment envelope, and the clinic is not falsely shown closed.
Source: Tulsa Health Department braces for an unknown future (2025-03-14)
TOWN-43-B · Check the Bag for Government
Tulsa
At a Tulsa grocery loading area, a warehouse worker peers into a shopping bag beside your parked van.
Fact: Oklahoma ended the state sales tax on qualifying groceries on August 29, 2024; local grocery sales taxes remain.
Fictional resident: a warehouse worker shopping after a shift — “State grocery tax is gone. Local tax stayed. I shook the bag to make sure. One level of government was still in there.”

Scene: The worker peers deep into a reusable bag of raw produce while holding a receipt; a current traveler looks over from beside the van. The search through ordinary groceries treats the remaining tax as something hiding at the bottom of the bag.
Editable overlays: “State grocery tax: $0” — First line beside the blank receipt.; “Local tax: still here” — Second line beside the blank receipt.
Source: Oklahoma Tax Commission: State Sales Tax on Food and Food Ingredients (undated)
TOWN-43-C · Freedom, Required Viewing
Tulsa
At a Tulsa bus-stop bench, a school bus driver compares the state’s video order with your route.
Fact: In November 2024, Oklahoma superintendent Ryan Walters directed schools to show students his video announcing a Department of Religious Freedom and Patriotism. Some districts refused.
Fictional resident: a school bus driver and parent — “Walters required schools to show his religious-freedom video. My kid asked if she could skip it. Excellent question for the civics final.”
Scene: A school bus driver closes a tablet with a blank screen beside travelers at a bus stop; a child’s plain lunch bag rests nearby without depicting compulsory prayer.
Source: AP: Oklahoma Superintendent Orders Religious Department Video (2024-11-15)
TOWN-44-A · Half the Benefits, Twice the Sandwich
Waco
At a Waco food pantry bench, a cook recalls November’s delayed food assistance.
Fact: On November 4, 2025, KWBU reported over 31,000 McLennan County residents lacked November SNAP access during the shutdown; half payments were announced, but arrival remained unclear.
Fictional resident: a restaurant cook helping at a pantry — “Washington announced half the benefits. I cut one sandwich into two. Same accounting method, but mine comes with crusts.”
Scene: A cook cuts a single sandwich diagonally on a clean plate beside travelers at the pantry bench; both halves are clearly the original amount of food.
Source: Central Texas Food Banks brace for surge after SNAP benefits cut (2025-11-04)
TOWN-44-B · Free Enterprise Had a Fence
Waco
By Waco’s suspension bridge, a delivery driver pauses while you eat some food.
Fact: Waco’s 1866 toll-bridge charter barred competing bridges and ferries within five miles. McLennan County bought it in 1889, and it became a free city crossing.

Fictional resident: a local delivery driver — “Texas gave this toll bridge a five-mile monopoly. Free enterprise first required a law banning the competition. The public later had to buy its way out.”
Scene: A delivery driver and traveler sit with food near the bridge approach; the now-open public crossing is central, with no invented current tollbooth.
Source: The Waco Suspension Bridge — Texas Historical Commission marker (1976)
TOWN-44-C · The Commandments Have Jurisdiction
Waco
At a Waco grocery bench, a school aide discusses Texas’s classroom-poster law.
Fact: Governor Abbott signed Texas’s 2025 law requiring Ten Commandments posters in public-school classrooms. Implementation faced legal challenges and was temporarily blocked in some districts.
Fictional resident: a school aide and parent — “Abbott required classroom Ten Commandments. My kid asked whether the rule against lying applies to campaign ads. We have been discussing jurisdiction.”
Scene: A school aide holds a rolled blank classroom poster beside a child’s unlettered drawing and a grocery bag; travelers sit nearby with some food.
